replacements.old: Before you buy
replacements.new:
Simplified issue, guaranteed issue and graded benefits

Final expense policies are usually sold in one of three styles. Insurers use different names for them, so read the terms of the policy you are offered, not just its name.

  • Simplified issue. The application asks health questions, and many plans do not require a medical exam. The insurer decides from your answers whether to offer the policy and at what premium.
  • Guaranteed issue. There are no health questions. The Virginia Bureau of Insurance life insurance guide says restrictions often apply if death occurs within the first two or three years after the policy is issued. It also says insurers that take all risks usually pay only the total premium paid, rather than the face amount, if death occurs within the first year or two.
  • Graded benefit. The policy pays less than the full amount if death happens during its first years, on a schedule written into the policy. See how a graded death benefit works.

The NAIC’s Life Insurance Buyer’s Guide notes that a policy that does not ask for detailed health information will usually cost more and provide less coverage than one that does. Which style you are offered is the insurer’s decision, made after it reviews your application. We cannot promise a style, an approval or a premium before then.

The free look period: time to review a new policy

After a new policy arrives, you have a set number of days to read it and return it. In Virginia, Va. Code § 38.2-3301 gives you 10 days from the date the policy is delivered to you. If you return it to the insurer or its agent within that time, with a written request to cancel, the policy is void from the beginning and the insurer must refund any premium you paid. A policy may give you a longer period. Other states set their own rules; the NAIC Buyer’s Guide says the period is usually 10 days after you receive the policy and is usually stated on the first page. Our state pages for Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, Texas, Louisiana and Florida list what we confirmed there; for other states, see the state pages below and the policy itself.

The contestability period

In Virginia, for the first two years, an insurer can look back at the application if a claim is filed. Va. Code § 38.2-3305 requires an individual life policy to become incontestable once it has been in force for two years from its date of issue during the insured person’s lifetime, except for nonpayment of premiums. The NAIC Buyer’s Guide warns that if the insurer finds false statements on the application after it issues the policy, it could reduce or cancel the coverage. Answer every health question truthfully, and read the application before you sign it. The contestability period is separate from the reduced-benefit years on a guaranteed-issue or graded policy.

Grace period, lapse and reinstatement

A missed payment does not end a policy right away. In Virginia, Va. Code § 38.2-3303 requires a grace period of at least 31 days after a premium is due, and the policy stays in force during it. The insurer may charge interest of up to 6% a year on the late premium, and if the insured person dies during the grace period, the unpaid premium may be taken out of the benefit. If the premium is still unpaid when the grace period ends, the policy lapses, as the Virginia Bureau of Insurance guide explains.

A lapsed policy can often be brought back. Under Va. Code § 38.2-3311, if a Virginia policy’s value was automatically used to buy other insurance that is still in force, and the policy was not surrendered and cancelled, it may be reinstated within three years of the default. You would give evidence of insurability that satisfies the insurer, pay the overdue premiums with interest (up to 6% a year) and repay or reinstate any other debt on the policy. Otherwise the policy’s own reinstatement terms apply. The Virginia Bureau of Insurance guide says most policies provide for reinstatement within three years from the date of lapse, and that you should expect to pay the missed premiums with interest and show you are still insurable. Policies in other states follow their own state’s rules, and the policy itself spells out its terms. If a payment will be late, call the insurer, or call us, before the grace period ends.

Who may not need final expense insurance

The NAIC Buyer’s Guide suggests starting with questions such as whether anyone depends on you financially and how your family would pay your final expenses and debts. Some people find they do not need a final expense policy:

  • Savings are already set aside for the funeral and last bills, and the family will be able to reach them.
  • Existing life insurance is enough to cover those costs. If the coverage is through work, the NAIC guide cautions that you may not be able to take it with you if you leave the employer.
  • A funeral is already prepaid through a contract with a funeral home. That is a different product with its own rules; see final expense vs. a prepaid funeral plan.
  • The real need is income replacement. If a family depends on your paycheck, a larger term life policy may fit the need better.

If you already have a policy and are thinking of replacing it, the NAIC guide says to compare the two first, keep in mind that changes in your health may affect a new policy, and not cancel the current policy until you have the new one.

Before you buy

replacements.old: Want to switch plans? See when you can change Medicare plans in West Virginia.
replacements.new:
West Virginia’s Medigap birthday rule

Since June 11, 2026, West Virginia has a Medigap birthday rule (House Bill 4869). If your Medicare Supplement policy has been continuously in force for at least 24 months, you can replace it once per calendar year, in an application period that begins on the first day of your birthday month and ends 60 days later. The new policy must come from the same insurer or an affiliated insurer and have the same or fewer standardized benefits. Source: West Virginia Insurance Bulletin No. 26-02, Offices of the Insurance Commissioner, read November 27, 2026. The full details, including the exception when your insurer no longer sells such a plan, are in our guide to the West Virginia Medigap birthday rule and other ways to change plans. Apply first and wait for approval before you cancel your current policy.
